record.paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
record.original_question: For the complete graph K_n, must every three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing in which each edge route has at most one bend have total volume Ω(n^3)?

evidence.quote: Two open problems for such drawings are: (1) Does every drawing of Kn have volume Ω(n3)?
Since Kn = Gn,n−1, any 1-bend drawing of Kn has volume Ω(n3), which answers the first open problem mentioned above.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ an axis-aligned box (a Cartesian product of three closed integer intervals) in $\mathbb{Z}^3$, and to each edge $uv\in E$ an axis-parallel polygonal route that starts on the boundary of the box of $u$, ends on the boundary of the box of $v$, consists of segments parallel to the coordinate axes, and is internally disjoint from all vertex boxes and from every other edge route. The drawing is called 1-bend if every edge route has at most one bend (i.e., consists of at most two axis-parallel segments). The volume of the drawing is the number of unit lattice cells in the smallest axis-aligned bounding box that contains all vertex boxes and all edge routes.

Let $K_n$ denote the complete graph on $n$ vertices. Prove or disprove: every 1-bend 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of $K_n$ has volume $\Omega(n^3)$.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem has been resolved affirmatively: it is established that any 1-bend 3-D orthogonal box-drawing of K_n requires volume Ω(n^3), as a consequence of a more general lower bound for drawings of dense graphs G_{n,n-1}.
